title: Iceland Votes on EU Membership as Trump's Greenland Pressure Looms, Kyiv Weapons Depot Strike Kills 37
subhead: Icelanders went to the polls in a knife-edge referendum on resuming EU membership talks, shadowed by US pressure over Greenland, while a Russian strike on a Kyiv weapons depot killed at least 37. Iran signaled it is in no rush to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

sections.heading: Iceland's Knife-Edge EU Referendum Closes Under Greenland's Shadow
sections.body:
Voting closed Saturday in Iceland's referendum on whether to resume membership negotiations with the European Union, with polls showing the outcome on a knife-edge and neither the 'yes' nor 'no' camp straying more than a few points from a 50/50 split, according to Al Jazeera and AFP. The vote comes 13 years after Iceland, then led by a Eurosceptic government, paused EU accession talks. The pro-EU Social Democratic Alliance, which currently governs, called the vote and has promised to honor whatever the public decides.

The referendum is being watched well beyond Reykjavik. AP reports that Trump's threats over Greenland have cast a shadow over the vote, with security, the sluggish Icelandic economy, and the future of the krona dominating the campaign. A 'yes' vote would likely trigger years of negotiations with Brussels and a second referendum on formal membership. Iceland is a founding NATO member and hosts the US military's Keflavik air base, making its alignment a matter of Arctic and transatlantic security.
sections.whyItMatters: A 'yes' would redraw Iceland's place in the European security and economic order at a moment when Arctic competition and US pressure on Greenland are intensifying.

sections.heading: Russian Strike on Kyiv Weapons Depot Kills at Least 37
sections.body:
A Russian strike on a weapons depot in the Kyiv area killed at least 37 people and forced hundreds to evacuate, the BBC reports. An investigation has begun into the storage of weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area, a decision that has drawn scrutiny after the deadly blast.

The strike is the latest in a pattern of Russian long-range attacks on Ukrainian military logistics and infrastructure. It comes as the war grinds through its third year with no sign of a diplomatic off-ramp, and as Ukraine continues to press its own deep-strike campaign against targets inside Russia.
sections.whyItMatters: The high civilian toll from a strike on a depot located near housing raises questions about Ukraine's munitions-siting practices even as it underscores the continued intensity of Russia's air campaign.

sections.heading: Iran Says It Is in No Rush to Reopen Hormuz as Economic Toll Mounts
sections.body:
Iran's deputy foreign minister said Iranian forces retain 'full oversight' of movements in the Strait of Hormuz and that Tehran is in no rush to reopen the waterway, according to Al Jazeera's live updates. The statement came as Iran's leaders publicly acknowledged the economic damage of six months of war with the United States.

President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that sanctions and the US naval blockade had caused exports and imports to slump by nearly 35 percent, Al Jazeera and Reuters report. He said Iran had managed to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived Memorandum of Understanding signed with Washington in June, when oil sales were briefly permitted. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared publicly since the war began in February, issued a written statement calling on the government to address inflation, unemployment and market pressures.
sections.whyItMatters: Tehran's public acknowledgment of a one-third collapse in trade, paired with its refusal to commit to reopening Hormuz, signals a leadership under strain but still unwilling to concede the strait as leverage.

sections.heading: Turkey and Somalia Free Hijacked Cargo Vessel as Piracy Resurges
sections.body:
Turkish and Somali forces freed a Cameroon-flagged cargo vessel that had been hijacked by pirates, with Somali authorities saying 14 pirates were killed in the 10-day operation, Al Jazeera reports. The rescue is the latest sign of resurgent piracy in the waters off the Horn of Africa.

Separately, Turkey summoned Ukraine's ambassador over attacks on two Turkish-operated vessels in the Black Sea this week, Al Jazeera reported. The incidents draw a NATO member directly into the maritime fallout of the Russia-Ukraine war, testing Ankara's careful balancing act between Kyiv and Moscow.
sections.whyItMatters: Piracy off Somalia and attacks on Turkish-flagged shipping in the Black Sea both threaten commercial sea lanes, forcing regional powers to respond at a time when global shipping is already disrupted by the Hormuz closure.

sections.heading: Trump's Venezuela Oil Deal Draws Skepticism Over Its Scale
sections.body:
President Trump announced that the US has reached a deal with Venezuela's interim government, led by Delcy Rodriguez, to take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves across 17 strategic fields, according to AP and Al Jazeera. Trump called it 'the biggest oil deal in world history.'

Details remain scarce, and analysts have questioned the headline number. Oil market researcher Rory Johnston called the 65-billion-barrel figure 'a red herring' with little relevance to any actual deals, noting the real terms are still almost entirely unknown, Al Jazeera reported. The deal would give the US government a stake in roughly a fifth of Venezuela's proven reserves, the world's largest deposit at an estimated 303 billion barrels.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal, if real, would give Washington unprecedented control over a major share of global oil reserves at a time of energy disruption — but the lack of fixed terms leaves its actual significance unclear.

bottomLine: The day's most consequential development is Iceland's knife-edge vote on EU membership, a decision shaped by US pressure over Greenland that could redraw Arctic and European alignment. Russia's deadly strike on a Kyiv weapons depot shows the Ukraine war's continued intensity, while Iran's acknowledgment of a one-third collapse in trade — paired with its refusal to rush the reopening of Hormuz — points to a Tehran under strain but still holding the strait as leverage. Piracy off Somalia and attacks on Turkish shipping add to the strain on global sea lanes. The Venezuela oil deal remains more spectacle than substance until its terms are disclosed.
